title: Janet Horne Executed at Dornoch: Last Execution for Witchcraft in Scotland
description: Janet Horne (sometimes identified as an unknown woman, as 'Janet Horne' may be a generic name) was burned at Dornoch in Sutherland in 1727, in what is generally accepted as the last execution for witchcraft in Scotland. She and her daughter were accused; the daughter escaped, but the mother — reportedly suffering from cognitive decline — was tried and burned. The Dornoch execution occurred nine years before the British Witchcraft Acts were formally repealed in 1736, illustrating that provincial Scottish practice lagged significantly behind both the legal repeal and the cultural shifts visible in London. A stone monument was erected in Dornoch in 1722 at the supposed execution site.
historiographical_note: The Janet Horne case is significant partly for its date — well after the decline of large-scale prosecution — and partly for the cognitive decline reportedly exhibited by the accused, raising questions about vulnerability to accusation. Brian Levack's work on the geography of Scottish witch prosecution has shown that the Highland periphery lagged behind the central belt in following broader cultural and legal trends.
source_method: Contemporary accounts; Scottish legal records; secondary scholarship on Scottish witch-hunting
scholarly_disagreement: The identity of the last Scottish execution is sometimes contested; some sources give 1722 or other dates for the last formal prosecution. The 'Janet Horne' name may be a generic placeholder used by sources compiled later.
